title: Red Families, Blue Families, One Crisis
author: Benjamin Mabry
summary: Benjamin Mabry, a guest essayist on Aaron Renn's Substack, draws on Darel Paul's typology of American family models — Blue, Red, and Creole — to argue that the political culture war between left and right over family values is misreading the data. Each model has its own distinct failure mode, and those failure modes are increasingly driven by economic and social forces rather than by the superiority or inferiority of either model's values. The Blue Model, which grounds marriage in a partnership of two individuals pursuing shared life-long projects, requires high socioeconomic status to function; when resources shrink and competing projects produce conflict rather than synergy, the partnership breaks and produces the 'failed Blue Model' of divorce among credentialed professionals. The Red Model, grounded in kinship, household, and a patriarchal symbolic structure, shows greater socioeconomic range but is more vulnerable to personality-driven failure; Red Model marriages can succeed in the working class and fail in the upper-middle class. Mabry's larger argument is that both models are under crisis not because either is intrinsically wrong but because the economic and social conditions that made each function are deteriorating.
points: The Blue Model grounds marriage in individual partnership aimed at shared life-long projects (career advancement, self-actualization, shared lifestyle preferences). It requires high socioeconomic resources to function; when those resources contract, competing projects produce partnership conflict rather than synergy.

The Red Model grounds marriage in household and kinship — a husband, wife, children, and extended family network. The Patriarch holds a symbolic unifying position even when not exercising the role practically. Personality characteristics (rather than class) drive Red Model failure, which means it can succeed in the working class and fail in the upper-middle class.

The political right cites Red failures (teen pregnancies, dysfunction in the Palin family) to mock Red values; the left cites Blue failures (self-actualizing divorce that harms children) to mock Blue values. Both moves mistake a model's failure mode for evidence of the model's inadequacy, ignoring the structural conditions that produce both.

Real families rarely exemplify one pure model: a predominantly Blue couple may still value extended family; a predominantly Red couple may care about building shared assets. The models clarify essential structures found in many observations rather than perfectly describing any particular family.

The insight the framework yields: distinguishing a model's failure from economic forces' effects on the model. Blue Model failure in the professional class is not evidence that the Blue Model is wrong; it may be evidence that the economic resources it depends on have become unequally distributed.
quotes: Conservatives post pictures of Mitt Romney, his wife, and many children and grandchildren to show the superiority of their family values. Liberals may well tout the marriage of Barack and Michelle Obama to do the same. What they really show is changes in our society that show up in different ways in Blue and Red families because of their distinct failure modes.

The Blue Model marriage sees family as a partnership between two individuals for the sake of shared life-long projects that may include developing a common domestic life, having children, saving for retirement, advancing one or both careers, or pursuing shared lifestyle preferences.
Blue Model family structure requires a high socio-economic status to function effectively and may fail when resources are strained between competing projects.

The Red Model marriage sees family as the primary social unit in a wider community which is primarily biological in character. A man takes a wife in order to have children within a context of related families in an extended community.

In Red Model marriages, the Patriarch has a central symbolic position as the unifying principle of household order and provider of stability, even if he does not in fact practice that role. Red Model families are the most diverse in terms of socioeconomic status.

Personality characteristics contribute more to Red Model failure than socioeconomic status; failed Red Model marriages are common even among the upper-middle class while they can frequently be successful among the working class.
